The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that the function $f(x,y)=6{x}^{4}{y}^{3}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨1,1⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1)-f(0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨1,1⟩-⟨0,0⟩) \\ 6-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1⟩ \\ 6 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨24{x}^{3}{y}^{3},\,18{x}^{4}{y}^{2}⟩, \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨24{{c}_{1}}^{3}{{c}_{2}}^{3},\,18{{c}_{1}}^{4}{{c}_{2}}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}6 & =∇f⟨c⟩\cdot ⟨1,1⟩ \\ 6 & =⟨24{{c}_{1}}^{3}{{c}_{2}}^{3},\,18{{c}_{1}}^{4}{{c}_{2}}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨1,1⟩ \\ 6 & =24{{c}_{1}}^{3}{{c}_{2}}^{3}+18{{c}_{1}}^{4}{{c}_{2}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{a}}{{y}_{b}-{y}_{a}} & =\frac{x-{x}_{a}}{{x}_{b}-{x}_{a}} \\ \frac{y-0}{1-0} & =\frac{x-0}{1-0} \\ y & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{2} & ={c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the equation $24{{c}_{1}}^{3}{{c}_{2}}^{3}+18{{c}_{1}}^{4}{{c}_{2}}^{2}=6,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}24{{c}_{1}}^{3}{{c}_{1}}^{3}+18{{c}_{1}}^{4}{{c}_{1}}^{2} & =6 \\ 42{{c}_{1}}^{6} & =6 \\ {{c}_{1}}^{6} & =\frac{1}{7} \\ {c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt[6]{7}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find ${c}_{2}={c}_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt[6]{7}}.$ So, the point $C$ that satisfies the mean value theorem is $(\frac{1}{\sqrt[6]{7}},\frac{1}{\sqrt[6]{7}}).$
